introduction_markdown:
**Duration: three hours.** Enter the information required in the boxes of the flap. Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. Verify that this booklet contains six questions, no questions are repeated and there are no blank pages. Inform the invigilator in case this booklet contains less than six questions, questions are repeated or there are blank pages so that the booklet should be changed. Blank spaces in this question booklet may be used for rough work. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Noiseless calculators may be used.

**Useful data:** $R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ or $0.082\ \mathrm{atm\,dm^{3}\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$. One atmosphere (1 atm) = 1 Pa = $1.01\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ (as printed). Relative atomic masses (RAM): C = 12.0, O = 16.0, S = 32.0, H = 1.0, Cl = 35.5.

The paper has three sections: Section A - Physical and General Chemistry (questions 1 and 2); Section B - Inorganic Chemistry (questions 3 and 4); Section C - Organic Chemistry (questions 5 and 6). All six questions are compulsory.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A compound of RMM $120$ contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. The percentage composition of carbon and hydrogen are $40\ \%$ and $6.7\ \%$ respectively. Calculate:

(i) The empirical formula of the compound.

(ii) Determine the molecular formula of the compound *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Empirical formula.** The percentage of oxygen is the remainder: $100 - 40 - 6.7 = 53.3\ \%$.

| | C | H | O |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mass in $100\ \mathrm{g}$ | $40.0$ | $6.7$ | $53.3$ |
| Moles (divide by RAM: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0) | $\dfrac{40.0}{12.0} = 3.33$ | $\dfrac{6.7}{1.0} = 6.7$ | $\dfrac{53.3}{16.0} = 3.33$ |
| Divide by the smallest ($3.33$) | $1.00$ | $2.01 \approx 2$ | $1.00$ |

**Empirical formula = $\mathrm{CH_2O}$** (empirical formula mass $= 12.0 + 2(1.0) + 16.0 = 30.0$).

**(ii) Molecular formula.** $n = \dfrac{\text{RMM}}{\text{empirical formula mass}} = \dfrac{120}{30.0} = 4$

Molecular formula $= (\mathrm{CH_2O})_4 =$ **$\mathrm{C_4H_8O_4}$**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Amines are considered as Lewis bases.

(i) What is a Lewis base?

(ii) Arrange the amines below in order of increasing basic strength starting with the least basic.

$\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}$, $\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}$

Explain the reason for your trend. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) A Lewis base** is a species that **donates a pair of electrons** (a lone pair) to form a coordinate (dative) covalent bond. In amines the lone pair on nitrogen is donated, for example to $\mathrm{H^+}$.

**(ii) Order of increasing basic strength (least basic first):**

$$\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} < \mathrm{NH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3NH_2}$$

**Explanation.** The basic strength depends on how readily the nitrogen lone pair is available for donation.

- In **methylamine**, the **$\mathrm{CH_3}$ group is electron-releasing** (positive inductive effect). It increases the electron density on nitrogen, so the lone pair is more available and $\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}$ is a **stronger base than ammonia**.
- In **phenylamine**, the nitrogen lone pair is **delocalised into the benzene ring** (overlap with the $\pi$ system), so it is **less available** for donation: phenylamine is a **weaker base than ammonia**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the reaction scheme below and answer the questions that follow.

![fig-1](gce-al-chemistry-2026-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_1.png)

(The scheme: $\mathrm{C_3H_6}$ reacts with $\mathrm{HCl}$ to give A; A reacts by (i) to give $\mathrm{C_3H_7OH}$ (D), which reacts by (ii) to give $\mathrm{CHI_3(s)}$, yellow; A also reacts by (iii) to give B, and B with $\mathrm{H^{+}/H_2O}$ gives $\mathrm{C_4H_8O_2}$ (C).)

(i) State the reagents and reaction conditions for the conversions (i) to (iii) *[3 marks]*

| | Reagents(s) | Reaction conditions |
|---|---|---|
| (i) | | |
| (ii) | | |
| (iii) | | |

(ii) Give the structures and names of compounds A, B, C, and D *[4 marks]*

| Compound | Structure and Name |
|---|---|
| A | |
| B | |
| C | |
| D | |

(iii) Using suitable chemical reagents and reaction conditions, stating your observations clearly, distinguish between the pairs of compounds below: *[6 marks]*

A: $\mathrm{HCOOH}$ and $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$

B: $\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}$ and $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Reasoning on the scheme.** $\mathrm{C_3H_6}$ is **propene**, $\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2}$. Adding $\mathrm{HCl}$ (Markovnikov addition) gives **A = 2-chloropropane**, $\mathrm{CH_3CHClCH_3}$. D ($\mathrm{C_3H_7OH}$) gives the **yellow solid $\mathrm{CHI_3}$ (iodoform test)**, so D contains the $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH){-}}$ group: **D = propan-2-ol**, which fits the hydrolysis of 2-chloropropane (step (i)). Step (iii) replaces $\mathrm{Cl}$ by $\mathrm{CN}$ to lengthen the chain by one carbon: **B = 2-methylpropanenitrile**, whose hydrolysis gives **C ($\mathrm{C_4H_8O_2}$) = 2-methylpropanoic acid**.

**(i) Reagents and conditions.**

| | Reagent(s) | Reaction conditions |
|---|---|---|
| (i) A to D | aqueous sodium (or potassium) hydroxide, $\mathrm{NaOH(aq)}$ | heat under reflux (nucleophilic substitution) |
| (ii) D to $\mathrm{CHI_3}$ | iodine and aqueous sodium hydroxide, $\mathrm{I_2/NaOH(aq)}$ (or $\mathrm{KI/NaOCl}$) | warm gently (about $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) |
| (iii) A to B | potassium cyanide, $\mathrm{KCN}$, dissolved in ethanol | heat under reflux (nucleophilic substitution) |

**(ii) Structures and names.**

| Compound | Structure and Name |
|---|---|
| A | $\mathrm{CH_3CHClCH_3}$ : 2-chloropropane |
| B | $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHCN}$ ($\mathrm{CH_3CH(CN)CH_3}$) : 2-methylpropanenitrile |
| C | $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHCOOH}$ ($\mathrm{CH_3CH(CH_3)COOH}$) : 2-methylpropanoic acid ($\mathrm{C_4H_8O_2}$) |
| D | $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3}$ : propan-2-ol ($\mathrm{C_3H_7OH}$) |

Equations: $\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2 + HCl \rightarrow CH_3CHClCH_3}$; $\mathrm{CH_3CHClCH_3 + OH^- \rightarrow CH_3CH(OH)CH_3 + Cl^-}$; $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3 + 4I_2 + 6NaOH \rightarrow CHI_3 + CH_3COONa + 5NaI + 5H_2O}$; $\mathrm{CH_3CHClCH_3 + CN^- \rightarrow (CH_3)_2CHCN + Cl^-}$; $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHCN + 2H_2O + H^+ \rightarrow (CH_3)_2CHCOOH + NH_4^+}$.

**(iii) Distinguishing tests.**

**A: $\mathrm{HCOOH}$ (methanoic acid) and $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$ (ethanoic acid).** Methanoic acid also has an **aldehyde group (it is a reducing agent)**, ethanoic acid is not.

- **Tollens' reagent** (ammoniacal silver nitrate), warm in a water bath: **$\mathrm{HCOOH}$ gives a silver mirror** (grey-black precipitate of silver); **$\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$ gives no change**.
- Alternatively, warm with **acidified potassium manganate(VII)**: the **purple colour is decolourised** by $\mathrm{HCOOH}$ (carbon dioxide formed), but **unchanged** with $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$; or warm with Fehling's solution: red-brown precipitate of $\mathrm{Cu_2O}$ for $\mathrm{HCOOH}$ only.

**B: $\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}$ (ethanamide) and $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}$ (ethylamine).** Ethylamine is a **base**, ethanamide is **neutral**.

- Dissolve each in water and test with **red litmus paper / universal indicator**: **$\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}$ turns red litmus blue** (universal indicator blue-purple, pH about 11-12); **$\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}$ has no effect** on litmus (neutral, pH about 7).
- Confirmatory test: add **copper(II) sulphate solution**: ethylamine gives first a **pale blue precipitate that dissolves in excess to give a deep blue solution** (complex ion, as with ammonia); ethanamide gives **no change** (the solution stays pale blue).
